name: Irish Potato Famine
kicker: A potato blight that starved Ireland · Mass death and emigration
briefing: When a water mold began rotting Ireland’s potato crop in 1845, the island’s poor lost their main food source. Over the next several years, about a million Irish men, women, and children died of starvation and disease, and roughly a million more fled overseas, many in crowded, disease-ridden “coffin ships.” The famine emptied whole villages and helped send waves of Irish immigrants to cities like Boston and New York.
answerHtml: Irish Potato Famine (or Great Famine, Great Hunger, or An Gorta Mór [“un GOR-tuh MORE”]; prompt on famine alone)

tossups.p: Civil servant Charles Trevelyan, who ran much of Britain’s relief effort during this crisis, wrongly treated it as a kind of divine punishment rather than an emergency needing aid. Journalist John Mitchel was convicted and exiled after attacking the government’s response to this disaster.
tossups.r: Desperate families fled overseas on crowded, disease-ridden “coffin ships” during this disaster. For 10 points, name this 1840s catastrophe in which a blight ruined Ireland’s potato crop.

tossups.p: The emigrant ship _Jeanie Johnston_ became famous for never losing a passenger on its Atlantic crossings during this disaster, unlike many of the overcrowded vessels that carried the starving abroad. Some Protestant missionaries offered food to hungry Catholic children who agreed to hear their teaching, a practice nicknamed “souperism.”
tossups.r: Prime Minister Robert Peel repealed Britain’s Corn Laws in 1846, partly in response to this crisis. For 10 points, name this disaster in which a blight struck Ireland’s potato crop beginning in 1845.

tossups.p: Even as people starved during this disaster, Ireland kept exporting other foods, such as grain and livestock, to Britain. Anger over the government’s handling of this crisis helped strengthen Irish nationalism and later calls for independence from Britain.

trap.title: Which “Great Famine”?
trap.body: Quiz bowl has more than one “Great Famine.” A European famine from 1315 to 1317, caused by terrible weather and crop failures, struck centuries before the potato even reached Europe. The Irish Potato Famine of the 1840s is a completely different, later disaster, even though both are sometimes called “the Great Famine.”
trap.fix: Potatoes, blight, coffin ships, Robert Peel, and the 1840s all mean the Irish Potato Famine. Bad weather, the start of the Little Ice Age, and the 1300s mean the earlier European famine instead. When in doubt, listen for the century.
